procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the High Court of Allahabad holding the dismissal of O. P. Gupta (respondent No. 1) from service invalid.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court held that the order of dismissal from service passed against respondent No. 1, O. P. Gupta, was invalid.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of U. P. filed Civil Appeal No. 1731 of 1967 in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment. The appeal was heard on multiple occasions, including February 22, 1969, and October 15-17, 1969. After the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, O.P. Gupta wrote, printed, published, and circulated a pamphlet criticizing the senior judge. The President of the Bar Association of the Supreme Court and three other Advocates filed a petition for contempt of court against O.P. Gupta and the printer/publisher of the pamphlet. The Supreme Court issued notice to the respondents to show cause why they should not be committed for contempt of Court. Respondent No. 1 filed applications challenging the maintainability of the petition and requesting to cross-examine the petitioners and summon evidence. The Court rejected the request for adjournment and directed the respondent to file an affidavit on merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the existing law relating to contempt of Court is a 'law' or not within the definition of the word 'law' in Art. (13)(3)(a) of the Constitution.

facts: An argument was made before the Court that the existing law relating to contempt of court is not a 'law' as defined by Article 13(3)(a) of the Constitution.
law: Article 19(2) of the Constitution permits the state to impose 'reasonable restrictions' on the right to freedom of speech and expression in relation to contempt of court.
application: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that it was "not necessary to decide" the point of whether the law of contempt is a 'law' under Article 13(3)(a).

The Court bypassed this question because it found that, in any event, the existing law of contempt imposes 'reasonable restrictions' on the freedom of speech, which is permissible under Article 19(2).
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the need to decide the issue, concluding that since the law of contempt was found to impose reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2), the preliminary question of whether it qualified as a 'law' under Article 13(3)(a) was unnecessary to resolve the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the existing law relating to contempt of court imposes reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression within the meaning of Art. 19(2) of the Constitution.

facts: A legal challenge was brought against the existing law of contempt of court.
The challenger (the first respondent) argued that this law imposes unreasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
law: Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution guarantees the right to freedom of speech and expression.
Article 19(2) of the Constitution allows for the imposition of 'reasonable restrictions' on this right in the interests of, among other things, contempt of court.
The existing law of contempt of court makes any publication that is calculated to interfere with the due course of justice or the proper administration of law an act of contempt.
application: The Court assumed for the sake of argument that Article 19(2) applies to the existing law of contempt.
The Court rejected the respondent's argument that scurrilous attacks on a judge after a case is decided do not affect the administration of justice.
It reasoned that such attacks have the 'inevitable effect of undermining the confidence of the public in the Judiciary.'
The Court stated that if public confidence in the judiciary is lost, the due administration of justice 'definitely suffers.'
The Court also noted that judges, by reason of their office, are precluded from entering public debates to defend themselves, making them vulnerable to such attacks.

Citing precedent (Lakhan Singh v. Balbir Singh), the Court affirmed that the law of contempt imposes reasonable restrictions and that conditions in India are different from those in the United States.
The Court concluded that the restrictions are in the public interest because they protect the administration of justice by maintaining public confidence in the courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the existing law relating to contempt of court imposes reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression, and is therefore valid under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petition for contempt was maintainable.

facts: The respondent filed an application arguing that the petition for contempt was not maintainable and should be dismissed.
One of the respondent's main arguments was that the substance of the allegedly contemptuous pamphlet had already been included in a writ petition he had previously filed.
The respondent also contended that the petition was filed with a vengeful motive, which itself was a form of contempt.
The court also considered the issue of delay in the proceedings.
law: Filing a writ petition containing certain allegations does not provide a legal defense for the separate act of committing contempt by circulating those same allegations in a pamphlet or booklet.
The power of the court to take action for contempt is not lost due to delay, even though delay is generally to be deprecated.
The alleged motive of the person filing a contempt petition does not render the petition non-maintainable if contempt has, in fact, occurred.
application: The Court found the respondent's argument that the material was already in a writ petition unpersuasive, stating it could not "appreciate this line of argument."
The Court reasoned that even if the allegations were in a prior court filing, the subsequent act of circulating them in a pamphlet was a distinct act that constituted contempt.
The Court dismissed the respondent's contention about the petitioner's vengeful motive, finding there was "no substance" to it.
The Court affirmed that its power to hear the contempt case was not extinguished by any delay in the proceedings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the respondent's arguments and held that the petition for contempt was maintainable. The Court concluded that neither the prior filing of a writ petition containing the same allegations, the alleged motive of the petitioner, nor any delay in the proceedings provided a valid defense or a reason to dismiss the petition.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petition for contempt was maintainable.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner implicitly argued that the petition was maintainable by filing it under Article 129 of the Constitution, seeking action against the respondents for contempt of the Supreme Court.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the petition was not maintainable because the judge (Mr. Justice Shah), before whom the alleged contempt occurred, did not choose to take any action at that time, making it improper for the petitioners to initiate proceedings later.

cases.principle: The general provisions of Article 19(1)(a) must yield to the special provisions of Article 194(3) and Article 105(3) concerning parliamentary powers, privileges, and immunities.

cases.case_name: Legal Remembrancer v. B. B. Das Gupta
cases.principle: The restrictions imposed by the law of contempt are reasonable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The restrictions imposed by the existing law of contempt are reasonable and in the public interest, and therefore do not violate the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.
obiter: The Constitution makes this Court the guardian of fundamental rights and it would not enforce any law which imposes unreasonable restrictions on the precious right of freedom of speech and expression.
It is not necessary to decide whether the existing law relating to contempt of Court is a 'law' within the definition of Article 13(3)(a) of the Constitution.
The Executive has not shown due diligence in complying with this constitutional provision.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found it unnecessary to decide whether the existing law of contempt is a 'law' under Article 13(3)(a) of the Constitution. It held that, assuming Article 19(2) applies, the restrictions imposed by the existing law of contempt on the freedom of speech and expression are reasonable and in the public interest, and therefore constitutionally valid.
legal_tests_applied: Reasonable restrictions test under Article 19(2) of the Constitution, which assesses whether limitations on fundamental rights are justifiable.

The test for what constitutes contempt by scandalizing the court, which is met if a publication attributes judicial dishonesty or leaves an ordinary reader with the clear impression that injustice was deliberately done on political grounds.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the contempt petition was not maintainable was rejected, as the court found that there is nothing in law which prevents this Court from entertaining a petition at the instance of the President of the Supreme Court Bar Association and other advocates.

The court rejected the challenge to the contempt law itself, holding that even if it is subject to fundamental rights, the restrictions it imposes on freedom of speech are reasonable and in the public interest.
why_respondent_won: The petition for contempt was deemed maintainable because the Bar is vitally concerned in the maintenance of the dignity of Courts and the proper administration of justice.
The court affirmed that the existing law of contempt imposes reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech, thereby upholding the legal basis for the contempt proceedings.
policy_considerations: The Bar is vitally concerned in the maintenance of the dignity of Courts and the proper administration of justice.

The Constitution makes this Court the guardian of fundamental rights conferred by the Constitution and it would not desire to enforce any law which imposes unreasonable restrictions on the precious right of freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by the Constitution.
The restrictions imposed by the existing law of contempt are in the public interest.
